item.title: Nvidia Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
item.description:
Nvidia said on Tuesday that its sales topped $100 billion for the first time in the third quarter, twice as much as a year earlier, while company officials made clear they have no interest in the return of co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned last week.

Mr. Huang and his allies have mounted a campaign over the past week to return him to the top of the company he started more than three decades ago at a Denny’s in Silicon Valley.

But in a call with Wall Street analysts on Tuesday, Harvey C. Jones, the chair of the company’s board, made clear that Mr. Huang is not welcome.

Mr. Jones said that Mr. Huang voluntarily resigned last week after reports of a relationship with a company customer and an employee, which Mr. Jones described as “personal behavior inconsistent with its code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.”

“The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.,” Mr. Jones said.

Mr. Huang, who turned Nvidia into the dominant producer of artificial intelligence chips, resigned following revelations he had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing.

During Tuesday’s call, Nvidia’s new leader, Colette Kress, the interim chief executive officer, signaled the company was moving on from both Mr. Huang and his business strategies.

She said Nvidia was no longer shipping its chips to China, which had been a priority for Mr. Huang. Last year, he cut a deal with President Trump to give the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of chip sales to China in order to win government approval to sell Nvidia’s H200 chip, an older generation product, to Chinese companies.

But China hasn’t shown much interest in buying them. Last quarter, the company sold about $2.4 billion in chips to China, a fraction of the company’s $115.8 billion in total revenue for the period.

While questions continue to swirl around the circumstances that led to Mr. Huang’s resignation, Tuesday’s earnings release amounted to the final testament of the artificial intelligence company’s breakneck growth under his leadership.

Under Mr. Huang’s direction, the company has claimed a 90 percent share of the market for A.I. chips. It has used its commanding position to report some of the most explosive growth in corporate American history. In its fiscal year 2023, it posted a profit of $4.4 billion. Last year, its profit topped $120 billion. This year, it is projected to eclipse $245 billion.

Nvidia continued that trajectory in the most recent quarter with profit and sales doubling from a year ago. The company reported sales of $115.8 billion and profit of $65.3 billion, exceeding Wall Streets expectations for $109 billion revenue and $60 billion in profit.

Nvidia’s share price rose more than 4 percent in after-hours trading.

“Our momentum is real,” Ms. Kress said. “Our commitment to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change.”

But Nvidia’s staggering business growth is now facing the biggest test in the company’s history. Mr. Huang is the tech visionary who engineered the company’s runaway success. More than a decade ago he bet that Nvidia should shift its focus from making graphics chips for video games to building technology to create A.I. systems. His foresight positioned Nvidia to be the biggest winner in the A.I. boom.

Mr. Huang’s resignation throws the future of that business into question. He ran a company with a flat organizational structure where he had 60 direct reports. He was the company’s chief technologist, chief sales officer and top lobbyist in Washington, where had become a close ally of Mr. Trump. He had no obvious successor.

On Tuesday, Mr. Huang said in a statement that he had received calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, suppliers and customers who urged him to return as chief executive officer.

But Mr. Jones told analysts that the board is “laser-focused” on driving Nvidia forward without its longtime leader. The board’s search for a new, permanent chief executive “will be thorough” and quick, Mr. Jones said, and won’t end before they find “exactly the right person.” Nvidia has hired an executive recruiting firm, Heidrick & Struggles, to help with the search.

The pressure campaign to reinstate Mr. Huang is one of several significant challenges for Nvidia’s board and Ms. Kress. On Monday, the Trump administration said that it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China’s ability to access advanced A.I. technology through data centers in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. The rule has the potential to cut into Nvidia’s sales, which have boomed in that region as a result of demand from Chinese companies.

The administration’s crackdown came in the wake of revelations about Megaspeed, the Singaporean data center firm that was created by Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with Mr. Huang. Firms like Megaspeed have been able to legally buy Nvidia chips for data centers in Malaysia, Thailand and elsewhere that are then rented back to Chinese companies. Some of those companies are suspected of smuggling chips into mainland China, which is prohibited.

Nvidia has said that it complies with the law and that there is no evidence of its chips being smuggled to China. China rejects the espionage claims. Ms. Huang hasn’t responded to requests for comment.

The rule change has the potential to slow Nvidia’s business. The company has never said how much revenue it generates from the region, but Culper Research, a short seller, estimated in a 40-page report that it could be as much as 20 percent of the company’s data center sales.

Nvidia’s once-soaring shares have fallen 16 percent this year, including a 27 percent drop in the month since The New York Times first reported that U.S. intelligence agencies’ surveillance revealed Mr. Huang had a close relationship with Ms. Huang, whom officials believe had been recruited to collect intelligence for the Chinese government.

Still, in the company’s financial statements, there were signs that Nvidia has more room to run. In the quarter that ended in October, revenue growth accelerated from the previous three-month period.

Mr. Huang’s exit raises questions about future growth, which Nvidia fueled through investments to fuel the A.I. boom. Gene Munster, partner at Deepwater Asset Management, a tech investment firm, estimates Nvidia has committed up to $250 billion to support new cloud companies and A.I. developers. The company receives 50 percent of the money back through chip sales.

Mr. Munster said Mr. Huang drove those deals and “believed it was the right strategy.” But now, he said, “There’s the possibility someone new comes in and says, ‘We’re not going to do this anymore.’ Growth could be hampered.”

The company said it expected revenue in the current quarter to top $130 billion. Wall Street analysts had projected sales of $125 billion.

“We have the best technologists on the planet with a world class road map,” Ms. Kress said. “It’s business as usual.”

Lauren Hirsch contributed reporting.

item.title: Japan Attempts to Revive an American Industrial Icon
item.description:
For years, the Edgar Thomson steel mill stood on the outskirts of Pittsburgh as a rusting symbol of faded American industrial power. Two years ago, the plant, opened by Andrew Carnegie in 1875, appeared to be on the brink of closure, threatening to take hundreds of jobs with it.

Today, however, the mill is being jolted back to life by an unlikely savior. Following a fraught $14.9 billion takeover of U.S. Steel by Japan’s Nippon Steel, a squad of translation app-wielding Japanese engineers has descended on the plant, armed with a multibillion-dollar mandate to drag the aging facility into the 21st century.

In the Mon Valley, an industrial region winding along the Monongahela River in southwestern Pennsylvania, land at the Edgar Thomson site is being cleared for a new steel rolling mill the length of five football fields. Inside the existing facilities, equipment is being upgraded, while engineers dispatched by Nippon Steel are introducing new and more efficient Japanese steel-making techniques.

In Mon Valley, “the excitement level is the highest I’ve seen it here in my 27 years,” said Ron Ferchak, a director at U.S. Steel’s Mon Valley Works. The hope, he added, is “that this will be an operation that will carry on for decades.”

Before Nippon Steel’s acquisition was approved in 2025, it faced more than a year of intense opposition. The Biden administration, a rival U.S. bidder and leadership of the steelworkers union all tried to block U.S. Steel from going to a foreign buyer. They warned that Nippon Steel would abandon U.S. Steel’s Pennsylvania plants once the deal closed, hollowing out America’s ability to produce steel needed by the defense industry.

More than a year later, such dark predictions are largely being disproved. Nippon Steel is busy making preparations for the new $3 billion mill that is expected to prolong the site’s life for decades. In total, the work is expected to generate thousands of jobs and more than $1.7 billion in economic activity for Pennsylvania.

If this project succeeds, industry analysts say, it could serve as a model for reviving American manufacturing after decades of offshoring and lagging domestic investment. Japan has long been known for its high quality, hyper-efficient manufacturing methods pioneered by companies like Toyota. Its companies have capital and know-how to deploy overseas, and, facing an aging, shrinking domestic market, they need access to the U.S. economy.

“Whether it’s for reindustrialization or to compete against Chinese overproduction, the U.S. and Japan are very structurally compatible,” said William Chou, deputy director of the Japan Chair at the Hudson Institute, a think tank focused on trade, economics and national security. Nippon Steel-U.S. Steel-style investments show how “Japanese expertise, capital and technology can reinvigorate U.S. manufacturing,” he said.

Before Nippon Steel’s investment, the Mon Valley Works was on the brink. U.S. Steel, which in 1901 was the world’s biggest corporation, had dropped down the ranks of top global steel makers in more recent decades. It had come under pressure from different directions: lower-cost overseas steel and domestic competitors with newer steel-making technologies. Without Nippon Steel’s investment, U.S. Steel’s chief executive said in 2024, it probably would have to shutter plants in the Mon Valley.

When engineers dispatched from Japan arrived in Pennsylvania more than a year ago, they were met with a surprising reality. The Edgar Thomson plant — where enormous, crane-borne ladles coated in mineral residue carry hundreds of tons of molten steel to be refined, cast and cut into slabs — gave the impression of having gone decades without fresh investment. Baked grease and powdery iron dust caked the heavy machinery, while flakes of silvery “mill glitter” coated the floor, a sharp contrast to Japan’s typically spotless mills.

At Mon Valley plants, modern technology was hard to find. At similar facilities in Japan, sophisticated equipment to automate processes and improve quality had steadily accumulated over the years. In the Mon Valley, “it is like how it was in the past,” said Takeshi Yamamoto, an operations expert dispatched from Nippon Steel. “In Japan, you have to extract improvements like wringing water from an already bone-dry rag, but here, there are so many things you want and need to do.”

At the Mon Valley plants, Mr. Yamamoto and four others from Nippon Steel found themselves having to set up lives far from Japan, in the suburbs of a city with no direct flights back home. They are a handful of the roughly 100 engineers and technical experts sent from Japan to do similar work at U.S. Steel facilities across the United States, from Osceola, Ark., to Gary, Ind.

“Living in the U.S. was not always easy, especially during my first winter,” Mr. Yamamoto said. Having visited the country only once before — on a trip to Hawaii — he struggled with his limited knowledge of English. He also missed his wife and three children, who remained in Japan.

Things improved for Mr. Yamamoto after Mr. Ferchak, the U.S. Steel director, took him under his wing. Mr. Ferchak, a Pittsburgh Steelers fan, brought Mr. Yamamoto and several Nippon Steel colleagues to football games and tailgates.

Initially, Mr. Yamamoto wondered why he was asked to meet near the stadium five hours before kickoff. “That was my first surprise,” he recalled. He and three other Nippon Steel employees joined Mr. Ferchak and his friends, donning Steelers jerseys, setting up tables of food and jumping into a rousing round of Flip Cup — the drinking game where players race to chug their beverages and flip their plastic cups upside-down.

“None of us had ever played it before, so we were terrible at first,” Mr. Yamamoto said. After several rounds, though, the Nippon Steel team improved, mastering the art of flipping a cup on just one or two tries. “It was the first N.F.L. game and first tailgate for all of us,” he said. “We had a great time.”

Side by side, they strike an unlikely profile — Mr. Ferchak towering, muscular and tattooed, beside the smaller, close-cropped and baby-faced, Mr. Yamamoto. Yet on the floor of the Edgar Thomson plant, the two have developed a seemingly intuitive rapport, with Mr. Ferchak periodically stepping in to interpret for others what Mr. Yamamoto is trying to convey.

More than a year into the revival project, changes are already crystallizing. Buildings are being torn down to make way for the new mill, which will enable U.S. Steel’s Mon Valley operations to produce about 3.5 million tons of sheet steel annually, up from its current 2.2 million tons. The mill will make high-strength steels for cars and other uses that Mon Valley sites were previously unable to produce.

Inside the existing Edgar Thomson facilities, new techniques are taking root. One example: Molten iron is blasted with oxygen to remove impurities as it is turned into steel. Japanese engineers introduced a new method to pause the blast mid-cycle, allowing the accumulated impurities to pour off. It’s a change that cuts down on costly chemical additives needed for further refining.

Already, the investments are bolstering recruitment at a mill built on generational ties, said Mr. Ferchak, a fourth-generation employee himself. “My son is a senior in high school now, so now I have the confidence to tell him that if he would want to choose this path, I think it’s a good choice,” he said. “A few years ago I may not have had that level of confidence.”

Nippon Steel’s acquisition allows it to sell into the U.S. market without the high wall of tariffs the United States places on imported steel. It also gained access to U.S. Steel’s newer and higher-tech manufacturing sites in Arkansas and Alabama.

But it also paid a steep price. Not only did the company spend enormously on the acquisition, it made a pledge to invest $11 billion in U.S. Steel facilities, including aging ones like in Mon Valley. The agreement also includes an unusual component demanded by President Trump in exchange for his approval. Under what is known as Trump’s “Golden Share,” the U.S. government holds authority to halt plant closures or mass layoffs.

“There’s no question that Mon Valley will be better off after this investment,” said Willy Shih, a professor of management at Harvard Business School, who has studied U.S. Steel’s operations. “Before the investment, it was technically obsolete,” he said. “The only question on my mind is, will Nippon earn a return on its investment?”

The United Steelworkers union has different questions. Union leadership, which had vehemently opposed Nippon Steel’s initial bid to acquire U.S. Steel, is now focused on making sure that the Japanese company keeps its promises.

“We’ve had some time now to judge Nippon by its actions,” Bernie Hall, a union director overseeing bargaining with U.S. Steel, said in a statement. “There’s been some progress, and we’re willing to acknowledge that.” At the same time, “promises alone don’t protect jobs,” he said. “Nippon made significant commitments, and we expect them to deliver on every one of them.”

For their part, U.S. Steel workers — at first cautious about a buyer most knew little, if anything, about — have largely come on board.

Initially, “they came in and just watched, observed, and asked questions and never really told us to change this or that,” said Vince Bruno, 39, a member of the union who has worked for 13 years at one of U.S. Steel’s Mon Valley plants. Then, gradually, executives and engineers from Japan began to gently make suggestions — like, “Hey, this might be helpful.”

Now, Mr. Bruno added, “we’re rolling better. Our quality is going up. Our yield numbers have gone up, and we’re just trying to see how much we can still get out of our mill.” He went on: “Before Nippon came in, we were asking, ‘What’s going to happen? Who’s going to get money? Who’s going to get shut down?’” At this point, “I can’t think of anybody who has anything truly negative to say.”

U.S. Steel workers are not the only ones embracing change.

Tomoki Hatao, another transplant in the Mon Valley, said he has discovered several work practices during his time at U.S. Steel that he hopes to take back to Japan. These include fewer, shorter meetings and a greater sense of individual ownership over tasks. Compared with the cumbersome decision-making process in Japan, he added, “the sense of speed really stands out.”

But importing these changes to Japan might have to wait. In the United States, Mr. Hatao said he has enjoyed having more time after work to spend with his family than he had in Japan. He has also been consistently surprised by how friendly Pennsylvanians are. And he likes the local microbrews.

“I would like to stay in the United States for as long as possible,” he said.

item.title: Capturing the Hustle of Unsung Jobs in New York City
item.description:
Times Insider explains who we are and what we do and delivers behind-the-scenes insights into how our journalism comes together.

A man who cleans the reflecting pools at the 9/11 Memorial. A Broadway actress who has learned seven roles by heart, not knowing which, if any, she’ll be asked to play on a given night. A cyclist who measures the New York City Marathon route with a low-tech device and spray paint, inch by painstaking inch.

These are just some of the unsung jobs that make life in New York City go round.

“It’s like a person you met at your nephew’s wedding,” said Bill Ferguson, an assistant editor on The New York Times’s Metro desk, which in September began publishing a series of features on individuals who perform some of the city’s jobs that you might not have thought even existed. “It’s like: ‘Did you meet the guy who repairs Citi Bikes? Oh, my God!’”

The idea for the series, New York at Work, came about last year when the photographer Juan Arredondo, who lost a cousin in the Sept. 11 attacks, was visiting the reflecting pools at the 9/11 Memorial in Lower Manhattan. He noticed a toy floating in the water. He got to wondering: Who takes care of this place?

“I wanted to capture the labor and the workers who make a city possible, and whom most of us never see,” said Mr. Arrendondo, who photographs the series.

In interviews last week, Mr. Arrendondo; Mr. Ferguson, who edits the stories in the series; and Eve Edelheit, who edits the photos and videos, shared what they aim to capture about the city through the stories, how they select the people they profile and what they’ve learned working on the project. These are edited excerpts from the conversation.

This isn’t the first time the Metro desk has done a column about interesting jobs in New York City. How are you aiming to differentiate it from past efforts?

BILL FERGUSON Juan has the most voracious eye of any photographer I’ve ever encountered.

EVE EDELHEIT He grew up in Hackensack, N.J., as well as in Colombia, and this was really his love letter to New York City.

I think sometimes people forget that the photographers we work with at The New York Times are journalists. This was definitely one of those moments where I felt Juan was being a journalist-comma-photographer and really thinking about telling stories in different ways.

As a photographer, I remember what it felt like to be treated as window dressing. And so I don’t want people to think that just because it’s a visual project, that a reporter isn’t an equal team player. I want the reporters to have a moment in the story, too, where they really feel like they’re writing the way they want to write and finding things that the visuals don’t show.

Is this a specific effort to really capture something distinctive about the city?

FERGUSON We’d like to focus on jobs that can happen only in New York — or at least primarily in New York.

EDELHEIT We’re trying to show the surprising side of things that we all appreciate or utilize in the city, and maybe don’t take time to think about.

JUAN ARREDONDO I’ve lived in New York for more than 15 years, and I’ve always believed that the city’s true character lives in its workers, so many of them immigrants like me.

Do you find the people first, or do you identify interesting job titles and then search for people who do them?

FERGUSON It starts with: Here is a thing that’s built into our life. Who makes that work? The hard part comes after the bright idea — that falls to Eve and Juan, who have to track down all the relevant authorities and gain their trust so we can invade their lives for a while. I’ve seen the spreadsheet. It’s not glamorous work.

What have you learned working on this series?

FERGUSON Everybody’s interesting. Everybody has a story.

EDELHEIT It’s been a great learning opportunity about narrative structure in storytelling and how it all comes together. And it’s been fun to just let my curiosity about the city run wild. I’ll walk by something and think, “Would that be a good job?”

My husband’s a runner, and so the story about the marathon came from my curiosity about who paints the blue line that runs the length of the race. The people we’re approaching know their topics the best, and so it’s been like unwrapping a present each time.

ARREDONDO I’ve learned how much of the city is awake while the rest of us sleep. Many workers begin their shifts in the dark, in rain and snow, hours before the city notices them, so I plan my days around their rhythm, not mine.

We spend about two days with each worker or crew. On the first day, I shoot on my own, learning the routine and earning their trust. A Metro reporter joins on the second day for the interview. Nothing is staged, and we ask the workers not to change anything for us. The best moments rarely arrive in the first hour. They come once people forget the camera, and the day starts to speak for itself.

Many of these jobs involve extensive manual labor. Do you think they’ll still exist 20 years from now? Do members of Gen Z or Gen Alpha have the desire to fill them, given how device-heavy a world we live in now?

EDELHEIT New York is constantly changing, but there’s such an appreciation for where it’s come from, and the historic institutions we have, that there will still be an appreciation for having a nicely polished brass mailbox at Grand Central. And, you know, someone’s got to do it.

What’s the most interesting job you’ve ever had?

EDELHEIT Honestly, this is the best.

FERGUSON I had a work-study job in college at Syracuse University, where I was taking ethnographic tapes from Margaret Mead or her compatriots, of, say, Maori prostitutes, on quarter-inch reels and recording them onto a different tape deck in this basement studio. I was barely qualified, and I didn’t know how interesting it was at the time.

ARREDONDO Before photography, I was an organic chemist and research scientist at Merck, so moving from the lab to the camera was a big leap. In a way, both require close observation, patience and precision. Photojournalism has been the most interesting job I’ve had.

This series is meant to highlight underrecognized jobs in the city. For some New Yorkers, these jobs may not seem so new or novel. What’s your response to that?

FERGUSON They may be right! Although the woman at the Museum of Modern Art who cleans van Gogh’s “Starry Night” by hand — that’s pretty novel.

But we’ve done only five so far, and we would love to have suggestions.

item.title: The U.S. Could Hit Its Debt Limit by February
item.description:
The United States could hit a cap on how much it can borrow to fund government spending as soon as February if Congress does not take action to raise or suspend the nation’s statutory debt limit, according to an analysis published on Wednesday by the Bipartisan Policy Center.

The think tank’s analysis previewed a looming fiscal showdown in Washington, as the government continues to borrow huge sums of money to fund its spending on everything from the military to retirement benefits.

The debt limit has plagued presidents from both parties for decades. The cap stems from a 1917 law that requires Congress to authorize how much the nation is allowed to borrow to fund its obligations. Republicans raised the debt limit by $5 trillion to $41.1 trillion as part of the tax cut package they enacted last year. That threshold is expected to be reached sometime in February or March.

At that point, the Treasury Department would need to deploy so-called extraordinary measures to stretch out how long the government has to avoid default. Those measures include suspending investments in savings plans for government workers and health plans for retired postal workers to allow the nation to continue paying its bills. The Treasury can also temporarily move money between government agencies and departments to make payments as they come due.

The Bipartisan Policy Center estimates that the “X-date” — the moment when the United States is unable to meet its financial obligations and might default on its debt — could come as early as August.

The deadline could put pressure on Republicans to try to forge an agreement over spending and the debt limit before Democrats take control of Congress in January. If they are unable to pass such legislation, President Trump will be forced to negotiate with Democrats next year to prevent the government from defaulting.

The national debt topped $40 trillion in August, a milestone that came faster than expected because of the cost of the tax cuts that Republicans passed and spending on the war in Iran. Despite pledges to reduce the debt by cutting spending and accelerating economic growth, it has continued to grow under Mr. Trump’s watch. Concerns about the debt rattled investors this year, raising borrowing costs and making it more expensive for Americans to buy homes and cars.

A debt limit standoff would put pressure on Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to come up with creative ways to manage the government’s cash flow. During previous debt limit fights, Treasury secretaries have even examined the lawfulness of minting a $1 trillion coin or revaluing the nation’s holdings of gold to market prices.

The Bipartisan Policy Center said the timeline for the X-date would depend on several factors, including interest rates, court decisions related to tariffs and economic growth. The timing will also be affected by the spending bill that lawmakers are working to pass before the end of the year.

It is possible that Democrats’ taking control of the House and the Senate could mean the end of a cap on what the United States can borrow.

Representative Brendan Boyle, the Pennsylvania Democrat in line to become the chairman of the House Budget Committee in January, told The New York Times this month that he would like to cut a deal with Mr. Trump to end what has become a perennial cycle of high-stakes fiscal clashes between the president and Congress that have repeatedly brought the country dangerously close to a federal default.

Mr. Boyle has long pushed for legislation that would allow the Treasury Department to suspend the debt limit, subject to congressional override, rather than requiring an affirmative vote by Congress to increase it.

“He wants it raised,” Mr. Boyle said of Mr. Trump. “We never again want to see a Democratic president have to have this held like a gun against their head, the same way it happened to Joe Biden and to Barack Obama.”

The idea has a chance of winning favor with Mr. Trump, who said last year that he agreed with Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, that the debt limit should be abolished.

“The Debt Limit should be entirely scrapped to prevent an Economic catastrophe,” Mr. Trump wrote on social media.

item.title: Europe Is Racing to Make Air Defenses ‘Cheaper Than What We Are Shooting Down’
item.description:
In June 2023, two young engineers in Munich, Balazs Nagy and Batuhan Yumurtaci, hopped in a car and set off on a 20-hour journey without telling their parents the destination.

This was no ordinary road trip.

Eager to use the skills they honed at the Technical University of Munich, the two drove to Kyiv to attend a hackathon focused on protecting Ukraine from Russian attacks. As they shared ideas in an underground parking lot, a drone slammed into the building next door. The experience clarified what they wanted to do next.

“That was the moment we were really convinced,” said Mr. Nagy, who started Tytan Technologies with Mr. Yumurtaci a few months later and leads the company as chief executive.

As the war in Ukraine approaches its sixth year and Russia’s hybrid attacks against Europe escalate, governments are calling on companies like Tytan to help plug gaps in the region’s air defenses. The industry is under pressure to increase production, lower costs and keep pace with threats that continue to evolve. Many companies are forging partnerships in Ukraine to capitalize on the country’s military technology expertise and gain crucial insights from the front line.

Mr. Nagy and Mr. Yumurtaci, now 32 and 30, are overseeing a fast-growing operation to produce small uncrewed aircraft that can destroy hostile drones. At a factory outside Munich, dozens of employees dressed in black have started assembling these interceptors, working beneath the flags of Germany, Bavaria, the European Union and Ukraine. Each one will be able to reach speeds of up to 250 miles per hour and altitudes of 16,000 feet.

The site will ramp up production to as many as 3,000 interceptors a month. Tytan expects demand to rise even faster. The company and its competitors are also seeking to upend the economics of defense technology. The goal: develop weapons that are “cheaper than what we are shooting down,” Mr. Yumurtaci said.

Backed by investors including the NATO Innovation Fund, Tytan has already cut the cost of its interceptors by half, he said, declining to be more specific. Russia’s versions of Iranian-designed Shahed drones cost $20,000 to $50,000 apiece, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated.

Underscoring the challenge, Russia launched more than 8,700 drones against targets in Ukraine in October alone — or one drone every five minutes, according to estimates cited by Tytan. Russia has also developed more destructive jet-powered drones that are too fast for most interceptors to catch. Ukrainian officials have said those drones can reach speeds of up to 370 miles per hour — roughly three times as fast as older models.

Tytan, which has signed contracts with the German military and customers in Baltic countries and Ukraine, has introduced a new rocket-boosted interceptor that can travel more than 310 miles per hour but can’t sustain that speed. Its next goal is developing technology that can take on jet-powered threats.

Tytan has joined the German defense technology companies Helsing and Quantum Systems in the effort to protect critical infrastructure and cities, working alongside established defense contractors such as Leonardo.

Leonardo, the Italian defense company, is developing a “security dome” called Michelangelo that would integrate technologies across Europe and rely on artificial intelligence to detect, track and neutralize missiles, drones and other threats.

The company aims to test part of the system in Ukraine by the end of the year, assessing its ability to fend off drones in dangerous areas, Lorenzo Mariani, Leonardo’s chief executive, said at the company’s headquarters in Rome. The tests follow a decision by Leonardo to open a new unit in Ukraine earlier this year.

Leonardo, he said, is discussing potential cooperation with Thales Group, the French company that is planning its own dome.

Quantum Systems, which raised $1.2 billion from Blackstone and other investors, said its agreement with the German government last month to supply tens of thousands of interceptor drones for Ukraine would also strengthen production capabilities to protect the broader region. Quantum is setting up new production sites in Lithuania, Estonia, Romania and Britain.

Helsing, backed by the Spotify founder Daniel Ek’s investment firm, has introduced an A.I.-based air defense system to help countries detect and respond to hundreds or thousands of drone and missile threats launched at the same time. The company said last month that it was also developing interceptor missiles designed to counter jet-powered drones — the technology Russia has used this year to pummel Ukraine’s capital. Each interceptor is expected to cost tens of thousands of dollars.

Helsing warned that Russia was building launch sites that put parts of the European Union within range of attacks.

Europe’s vulnerabilities have been exposed by drone incursions, cyberattacks, sabotage and plots to kill executives of European defense companies. Britain recorded about 340 drone incidents near defense ministry sites in the year through August, while Germany identified 165 sabotage attempts between January and August, according to estimates cited by the Atlantic Council, a research group.

Russia sees hybrid conflict, hostile acts that stop short of open warfare, as the most effective means of weakening European support for Ukraine and believes the region lacks a “credible” deterrent, said Maksym Beznosiuk, an analyst at ACLED, a nonprofit that tracks global conflict. In the coming months, he said, Russia’s hybrid attacks are expected to intensify, especially along NATO’s eastern flank and in countries that are the biggest providers of military and economic aid to Ukraine.

“Europe is not moving fast enough,” he said.

The German government blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack in August at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The next month, a Russian drone struck a passenger train at a station near the Ukrainian border with Poland, hitting close to departing foreign visitors including the former C.I.A. director David Petraeus.

Many European countries are out of step with the “really fast defense tech innovation cycle we’re witnessing in the battlefields of Ukraine,” said Pavlo Zvenyhorodskyi, a senior research analyst at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. Combining Ukraine’s know-how with the financial and industrial strengths of companies across Europe is crucial, he said.

A proposed Europe-Ukraine air defense system, called Freyja, is one part of the strategy. The project could help reduce the region’s dependence on the United States and provide a lower-cost alternative to American Patriot interceptors.

Another priority is ensuring the industry’s suppliers have the capital they need to keep up with rising demand, said Mr. Mariani, Leonardo’s chief executive. As the continent increases military spending, the sector is encountering supply-chain bottlenecks in areas such as missile propulsion systems, he said.

“The initial ramp-up has been achieved quite easily,” he said. “The second step — the scale-up — this is a real challenge.”

Many uncertainties remain, but some things are easier for Mr. Yumurtaci to predict: Drones will be the first technology used in the next conflict, while “we can already imagine in five to 10 years the entire battlefield will become completely autonomous,” he said.

European officials, he said, must ask whether the region can withstand an onslaught of hundreds of drones launched every night or an assault like the audacious drone attack Ukraine pulled off deep in Russian territory in 2025.

“Are we really ready to defend ourselves?” he asked.

item.title: Hospitals Rush to Patch Java Vulnerabilities
item.description:
Health networks across the United States rushed to secure computer systems after the discovery of a vulnerability in ubiquitous Java software, searching for signs of intrusion and applying patches that Oracle, Java’s owner, issued as a rapid fix.

The American Hospital Association said it was not aware of any negative impacts on hospital operations, other than the disruption of racing to respond to potential threats with new defenses.

Technology departments were in a race to “patch before they hack,” said John Riggi, the association’s national cybersecurity adviser. Recent system failures including air traffic control, banking and Microsoft software programs, Mr. Riggi said, “have placed hospital cyber teams at an unprecedently high security posture.” The causes of those failures are under review.

“Hospital cybersecurity teams across the country are using sophisticated tools to actively scan their entire internal networks, medical devices and internet-facing programs, searching for instances of the identified Java vulnerability, and patching as soon as possible,” Mr. Riggi said.

The health care industry has been under siege for years by ransomware attacks that have paralyzed their systems while hackers demanded payments of millions of dollars.

Hospital executives rarely disclose whether they paid the ransom, but their settlements in patient class-action lawsuits provide a means of tracking the phenomenon. The health care industry had the highest number of federal court settlements of any sector from 2010 to 2025, with 118, according to a new analysis by Cornerstone Research.

Hospitals use Java in several ways. With its patch on Tuesday, Oracle listed 21 products for which it should be used. Oracle bought Cerner, a large electronic health records vendor, in 2022.

Epic Systems, the largest health records vendor, said Tuesday that its systems were not affected. Judy Faulkner, Epic’s founder and chief executive, disclosed in September that Epic’s own system analysis using artificial intelligence tools had uncovered a flaw that could allow hackers to enter health records systems and possibly change data undetected. It issued a patch.

On Tuesday, consulting and group-purchasing companies for hospitals said that thousands of clients were working around the clock to secure systems. The use of A.I. to examine system integrity and in hacks has dramatically accelerated the pace of cybersecurity response.

“This is the crazy world we live in,” said Florian Quarré, chief data and A.I. officer at Premier, a group purchaser. “This came out hours ago, and is another example of a crack in well- wielded armor that is cracked open with new tools.”

He said the incident had exposed “the complexity related to these flaws in modern systems, the velocity at which they are found and the speed at which they are exploited.”

Security specialists must assume that hackers are using A.I. to exploit flaws in hospital systems, the experts said.

“The key is to move with urgency, follow the evidence as the threat evolves and focus resources where they can meaningfully reduce risk,” said Juli Rhoden Cunningham, chief information security officer at Vizient, a health care consulting company.

Mr. Riggi of the hospital association said that hospital technology teams have been on heightened alert for weeks. Among other cases, he cited a recent hack of the blood storage unit temperature systems in France.

item.title: Google Buys Worker Data From Spirit Airlines in a New Market to Feed A.I.
item.description:
When Spirit Airlines shut down in May, its assets went up for sale: a small fleet of airplanes, coveted slots at LaGuardia Airport and decades of internal workplace data, including employee records, tax forms, 100 million emails and half a billion Microsoft Teams messages.

Google had the winning bid, $10 million, for those employment records, a novel asset class the company said it would use to improve its artificial intelligence products. Imagine what a large language model could glean from the recruiting and timekeeping files of such a large company, or from workers’ snarky chats about their bosses.

But in August, a union representing 5,500 flight attendants affected by the bankruptcy filed an objection in federal court, saying that de-identifying measures promised by Google and Spirit, largely related to the protection of consumer data, were not enough to protect Spirit’s employees.

“If it was not for our union, this would have just happened in a fire sale in the middle of the night,” said Sara Nelson, the president of the Association of Flight Attendants. “This is a brand-new frontier for workers’ rights. It’s making people’s lives, their entire privacy, a commodity.”

Last week, Google agreed to new limitations on the employee data. In a hearing on Tuesday, a bankruptcy judge in federal court in New York State accepted the revised sale terms, and the flight attendants’ union dropped its objections. A spokesman for Google said the company was happy with the result but declined to comment further until the court posted the full language of the agreement.

Data has been sold before in bankruptcies that have raised consumer privacy concerns, like the 2025 bankruptcy of 23andMe, a genetic testing service. And there are examples of a failed company’s records becoming public. After Enron, an energy company, collapsed in 2001, federal investigators released a trove of company emails. They have been mined for case studies and research.

But only recently have companies sought access to a failed company’s internal work force data. There is a market developing, largely out of sight, for the carcasses of dead companies to be turned into feasts for large language models with insatiable appetites for written communication. SpaceX’s A.I. unit has considered buying data from struggling start-ups, Bloomberg reported in September.

The Spirit case appears to be the first large-scale example of using “corporate detritus” to train large language models, said Greg Ewing, a partner at Spencer Fane, a law firm.

“This is a whole new world, where all that data is so valuable to A.I. companies,” Mr. Ewing said. “We are going to see whole marketplaces arise out of it.”

Eric Chafetz, a partner at Lowenstein Sandler, a law firm, said the Spirit case was the first large bankruptcy sale in which a buyer had said it was motivated to build A.I. models. “We have recently received numerous unsolicited inbound inquiries from entities purporting to want to buy similar types of data,” he said. “Parties do believe there’s real value in trying to purchase a failed or failing company’s data.”

This has consequences for employees, Mr. Chafetz said: The bankruptcy code’s privacy protections were designed for consumers. “Employees aren’t in that picture at all,” he said.

Ms. Nelson said personnel files, even if they were cleared of identifying information, could be used to connect private data to a specific employee. A woman’s leave for reproductive care could one day be traced back to her. A pilot’s detailed background check, later uncovered, could expose sensitive personal details.

The flight attendants’ union, which is part of the AFL-CIO, wants to enshrine worker privacy protections into contracts and the law, she said.

“These are standards that can be put into law right away because we already have a major company working on the advancement of these A.I. models, who can comply with these very high standards of protections for workers,” Ms. Nelson said.

The union was joined in its efforts by other unions affected by the Spirit bankruptcy; in all, Ms. Nelson said, about 17,000 workers had been affected by the data privacy issue. In October, more than 120 congressional leaders sent a letter to Google and Spirit asking them to include more protections for employees.

The revised agreement makes clear that certain information is not to be part of the sale, including employee medical and disability records, flight crew fatigue reports and payroll records.

Last week, lawyers for GE Aerospace and CFM International, parts suppliers to Spirit, asked the bankruptcy court to exclude data related to their companies, too, including information related to engine maintenance and avionics systems.

“The data sale poses significant risks to parties that provided such information to the debtors over the years, because Google may use or disclose it through its A.I. products,” they wrote.

item.title: Christine Lagarde on Why She Stepped Down Early From the E.C.B.
item.description:
Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, warned on Wednesday that trust was “in short supply” around the world even as it remained fundamental to technology, trade and finance.

“We have to make every effort to secure it, to cherish it and to develop it,” she said in her interview with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the DealBook Summit.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Ms. Lagarde talked about her decision to step down early from her role at the central bank. As president of the bank, which sets interest rates for the 21 countries that use the euro, she has to observe strict political neutrality, something she said she wanted to shed. She’s leaving the role in February, about eight months early and critically ahead of presidential elections next spring in her home country, France.

Ms. Lagarde said she wanted to use her voice and decades of work in international finance against what she said was “fake news” and “misrepresentations” in European elections. “I see it as my duty to clarify, rectify and speak from my position and based on the experience that I’ve had,” she added.

She said that running the World Economic Forum, which hosts the influential annual gathering in Davos, Switzerland, “is one of the options” she is considering to do next. But she didn’t hint at other options, saying she wasn’t going to entertain more speculation while she is still E.C.B. president. “But I’m not retiring,” she added.

Ms. Lagarde also spoke about artificial intelligence and its dominance in the global economy today. It was one reason the European economy has been surprisingly resilient to the fallout of the war in the Middle East, she said. It was also partly why trade has risen in the past couple of years, despite President Trump raising tariffs on many countries.

The companies building A.I. equipment are all over the world, including in Europe. so there is not just a duopoly of dominance between the United States and China, she argued. “We are all in this together,” she said.

But she added that A.I. was highlighting concerns about fairness and the distribution of wealth. She alluded to the Anthropic I.P.O. taking place Thursday, which is set to value the company at more than $1 trillion, making it one of the largest public listings ever. “It raises the question of who is benefiting, how that creation of value will be shared and distributed,” she said.

item.title: A.I. Bubble Talk Enters the Conversation at DealBook Summit
item.description:
As tech stocks wavered Wednesday morning, conversation at the DealBook Summit turned to bubbles and sky-high valuations for artificial intelligence companies aspiring to go public.

As for the bubble question, opinion differs.

Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank, told Andrew Ross Sorkin in a morning session that she believed there was a “very ambitious price valuation which stands to be corrected eventually.” On the flip side, Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, one of the world’s leading A.I. companies, said there might be “ups and downs of valuations here or there,” but the overall “trend is going to be strong.”

item.title: OpenAI Executives Say They Have to Strike a Balance Between Safety and Progress
item.description:
OpenAI’s chief executive said Wednesday that pushing the safe advancement of artificial intelligence comes with inherent trade-offs, and the company had to strike a balance between prioritizing safety while continuing progress on developing A.I.

“We’re not going to be able to make everybody happy,” Sam Altman said at the DealBook Summit

If OpenAI only focuses on being “max pedal to the metal,” he added, “People will say, ‘Well, you know, please don’t kill us all.’”

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, has been under heightened scrutiny in recent months after its A.I. agents went rogue and hacked companies, including the open-source A.I. platform Hugging Face, and government systems.

Those were learning experiences, Mr. Altman said. OpenAI follows “iterative deployment,” he added, and the “only way that we have known how to make this technology safe is to confront reality,” suggesting that the risks couldn’t be known without having been tested in the real world.

OpenAI, along with other A.I. companies, has signed a voluntary agreement to conduct risk reviews and work with third-party evaluators. The company said on Monday that it was embedding independent safety researchers from third-party groups, including METR and Apollo Research, to evaluate OpenAI’s models against various safety measures.

“The models are now capable enough that we need to think about safety, security, alignment — that’s new. And that’s actually been a huge cultural shift,” said Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president and co-founder. “It’s not any one company. It’s really a whole industrywide shift.”

With its rival Anthropic on the verge of a public offering, Altman said OpenAI was still advancing toward its own I.P.O. “We plan to be a public company at some point,” Mr. Altman said.

Mr. Brockman has an equity stake worth at least $30 billion in OpenAI, but Mr. Altman famously owns no shares in the giant start-up. “When we were first setting up the structure, I said to him, ‘You should take equity,’” Mr. Brockman said, referring to the C.E.O.

“I should have listened to Greg,” Mr. Altman said, eliciting laughter. But he said that not having equity had not affected his work at OpenAI. “I don’t think you could argue that I have not acted with full commitment to the company.”

Mr. Brockman drew a contrast between his company’s structure and that of Anthropic, where the seven co-founders hold 50.1 percent of total voting control. “We’re the only company where the founders don’t have super majority control,” he said.

Mr. Altman has previously said the company is delaying its I.P.O. plans till next year to focus on safety issues. Earlier this month, OpenAI raised $11 billion as part of a fund-raising round valued at $1.25 trillion. That’s lower than the $30 billion it initially sought to raise at a valuation as high as $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic is expected to list its shares publicly on Thursday in what could be the world’s largest I.P.O. Earlier this month, Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, which would value the company at $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion.

item.title: Mark Carney Says Canada Will Not Back Down in Trade Talks With U.S.
item.description:
Canada’s relationship with the Trump administration continues to look frosty. But its efforts to bolster ties with China are showing promise.

Appearing remotely from Shenzhen, China, after long day of meetings, including a session with President Trump, Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada said at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday that Canada would not back down in its trade battle with the United States.

On the other hand, he said talks with China were “going exceptionally well.”

“We reached an agreement, we reduced tariffs in over 90 percent of trade irritants,” he said. “And of course, I’m speaking about our trade negotiations with China. They’re very professional. They move forward in a very linear fashion.”

He added: “Now, if you’re asking about the United States, well, we continue to have a series of issues there.”

Mr. Carney is wrapping up an eight-day tour, which has taken him from Ireland to the Philippines, Cambodia and finally China for the APEC summit. All of it in the cause of diversifying Canada’s economy away from its heavy dependence on the United States.

Asked if he now trusts Xi Jinping, China’s leader, more than Mr. Trump, Mr. Carney offered an indirect reply. “We look for situations where there is alignment, and we trust alignment,” he said.

Mr. Carney emphasized, as he has in the past, that Canada’s expanded relationship with China would have careful guardrails. And he dismissed the idea that Canada’s growing relationship with China would leave Canada trading one dependence for another, saying, for example, that he did not think selling canola, an oil seed, to China would be “compromising our sovereignty.”

Before a leaders’ dinner Wednesday evening in China, Mr. Carney had an unscheduled meeting with Mr. Trump. It did not advance Canada’s cause in the trade talks, the prime minister said.

“We had a very nice discussion this evening, so I’ll hang on to that,” Mr. Carney said. “Look, has it changed? I would say no is the short answer.”

Any resolution of the trade war, which had place tariffs of up to 50 percent on Canadian auto, steel and aluminum exports, will take a major change in policy in Washington, Mr. Carney said. The prime minister also rejected Mr. Trump’s repeated assertions that Canada had no leverage in negotiations with Washington.

“Our cards is that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us,” he said.

item.title: David Ellison Confirms Elon Musk Invested in Skydance
item.description:
David Ellison, the chief executive of Skydance, confirmed at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday that Elon Musk had invested in his media goliath, which was born out of a $110 billion deal combining Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery earlier this year.

“He doesn’t invest in a lot of companies,” Mr. Ellison said of Mr. Musk. “So to have his vote of confidence, and to have him as a shareholder, is an honor and a privilege.”

Skydance closed its acquisition last month, aided by a personal financial guarantee by David Ellison’s father, Larry. In addition to Mr. Musk, several other investors helped to contribute equity to the deal, lightening Larry Ellison’s personal load. Three sovereign wealth funds committed $24 billion and Laurene Powell Jobs invested $250 million.

Still, Mr. Musk’s investment, reported to be around $1 billion, brought attention in part because of Mr. Musk’s growing media influence as the owner of the social media platform X. Mr. Musk leads Tesla and SpaceX, which operates Starlink, the internet satellite service. There has been speculation that Starlink might offer Paramount content on its service, which is used by a number of airlines.

Mr. Ellison left the door open to future collaboration with the tech mogul. It would be “a privilege,” he said, “if there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future.” Still, he added, “there’s nothing that we can comment on.”

Mr. Ellison also spoke about his father, who is the founder of Oracle. Larry Ellison is friends with Mr. Musk and is a past investor in his companies, having committed about $1 billion to Mr. Musk’s deal to buy Twitter.

David Ellison said he was raised by “a single mother” after his parents’ divorce when he was 3 years old. As a youth, Mr. Ellison said, “We saw each other, you know, once a year, every other year.” That later changed: “Couldn’t be closer now.”

item.title: Nvidia’s Interim C.E.O. Tries to Soothe a Rattled Company: ‘We’ve Got This.’
item.description:
Shortly after 9 a.m. local time on Wednesday, Colette Kress, Nvidia’s interim chief executive, took the stage inside the company’s headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., and tried to exude calm.

It had been barely six days since she assumed the top job of the wildly profitable chip maker that has been rocked by revelations that its charismatic and visionary co-founder had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing. The all-hands meeting that Ms. Kress and other executives had convened, a livestream of which was reviewed by The New York Times, was an attempt to soothe the anxieties of a rattled company.

“Our ambition will not change,” Ms. Kress said, who sounded calm and confident as she sat perched on a stool. “Our passion to innovate will not change. Our commitment to customers, partners and shareholders will not change.”

She added: “Just remember, we’ve got this.”

In a the span of a month, Nvidia employees have learned that Mr. Huang had multiple affairs and had misled the board about behavior that was at odds with the company’s “code of conduct, standards and cultural norms.”

Mr. Huang resigned in the wake of those revelations, shocking people from Silicon Valley to Washington to Beijing, many of whom had come to see him as the figurehead of the A.I. boom. Nvidia’s market value, which was within a whisper of $6 trillion a month ago, has plummeted to $3.66 trillion.

Last week, Nvidia’s board named Ms. Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, as its interim chief executive. It has hired a search firm to find a permanent leader. It also is moving forward with an independent investigation, led by Wachtell Lipton, an outside law firm, into Mr. Huang’s behavior.

Mr. Huang and his allies have mounted a campaign over the past week to return him to the top of the company he started more than three decades ago at a Denny’s in Silicon Valley.

In a call with Wall Street analysts on Tuesday, Harvey C. Jones, the chair of the company’s board, made clear that Mr. Huang would not return.

The back and forth has left employees confused. Some have rallied behind Mr. Huang, signing letters and writing social media posts in support of his return.

“Jensen touched every single employee on an emotional level, genuinely cared about every single developer, and cherished every fragile research idea,” Nik Spirin, an A.I. engineer at Nvidia, wrote in a social media post. “He was both the soul and the mind of the company and the ecosystem.”

Others are looking forward to a future without him. Over the past year, Mr. Huang has alienated parts of this work force by allying himself with President Trump and undermining a plan by other tech companies to develop a systematic way to evaluate the safety of A.I. systems before their release, said three current and former employees who were not authorized to speak publicly about internal company matters.

Wednesday’s meeting began with video footage of company leaders making speeches and demonstrating products. The audio over that video included words that seemed relevant to the moment:

“Nvidia has a history of persevering.”

“It’s all about tenacity as a company.”

“This is the most incredible company on the planet.”

Ms. Kress then took the stage with the executive team and read written remarks. She praised the team behind her, saying “I know this team. I know how much they care for the company and the work.”

Ahead of Nvidia’s all-company meetings, the leadership team solicits questions from employees. The questions on Wednesday largely focused on Mr. Huang’s resignation.

Mr. Jones joined Ms. Kress onstage and shared details of his own Nvidia journey. He joined the board in 2004. He spoke about how his personal relationship with Mr. Huang had made the chain of events over the past week difficult for the board.

“The board was and is fully aware of Jensen’s monumental contribution to the company,” Mr. Jones said. “Several of the board, including me, worked with him for many years and counted him as a friend.”

Mr. Jones reiterated what he told Wall Street analysts on Tuesday.

“It is unrealistic to think we can find a Jensen clone,” Mr. Jones said. “He was one of a kind. That said, there are dynamic leaders out there with demonstrated intellect, high tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility and a track record of success.”

Chris Malachowsky, a Nvidia co-founder, choked up as he spoke about the situation the company has found itself in and thanked the board for its leadership. Then, he recounted how in the company’s early days, he, Mr. Huang and fellow co-founder Curtis Priem spent much of their time talking about the culture they wanted to instill in Nvidia.

They had a series of core values, he said. Maintain the highest standards in everything they do. Be intellectually honest. Innovate in everything they do. Be direct and candid in communications.

“Those have stood the test of time,” Mr. Malachowsky said. “I’m proud of them. In fact, it’s the violation of the first that’s given me pause over the past week.”

Mr. Malachowsky said that if the company adheres to those core values, it “will come out strong.” He urged employees to demonstrate those values in meetings and discussions.

“Keep these standards,” Mr. Malachowsky said. “Keep the culture alive. If we did our jobs well, and I think we did, we’re going to be fine.”

Ian Buck, the head of Nvidia’s data center business, said that the company didn’t need to worry about the road map it has developed for designing and manufacturing future generations of A.I. chips, which are the bedrock of the company’s business. He pointed to the leadership team beside him onstage and said, “We know how to get it done.”

Nvidia’s executive team said their business strategy won’t change. They plan to continue to support open models and close its acquisition of Hugging Face, a library of open A.I. models that Nvidia is purchasing for $12.9 billion. It is going to use those systems in its development of robotics and autonomous vehicles.

“All of that continues so we can become the leader of open models,” said Dwight Diercks, senior vice president of engineering.

Other executives made assurances about other key areas of the company’s business. They said Nvidia will maintain strong relationships with suppliers like Taiwan Manufacturing Semiconductor Company, which makes all its chips. They said the company would continue to outpace the industry in developing more powerful A.I. chips. And they will execute “a great business plan that endures.”

Nick Parker, who leads worldwide sales, said the company will expand its leadership ranks because it is “a great piece of the magic of how Nvidia delivers value.”

The leadership team had the benefit of the company’s latest earnings behind it. On Wednesday, the company reported quarterly profit and sales doubled, with revenue topping $100 billion for the first time. The results showed that the dominant maker of A.I. chips has momentum as the A.I. boom continues to expand.

The company said it will proceed with its Washington conference in December, which is scheduled the same week Mr. Huang and Tim Teter, the company’s general counsel, are expected to testify in a closed-door briefing with Congress. Mr. Huang is usually the ringmaster at those events. In his absence, other leaders at the company will share the stage for the keynote.

Ms. Kress, who joined the company 13 years ago, closed the nearly hourlong meeting by talking about her love of American football. Her son, who has been a student at the University of Florida, took her to a Gators football game. She marveled at the team’s third quarter tradition. when every fan in the stadium stands up and sings the team’s adopted anthem.

“It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony, singing that song,” she said. “You know what: We’re going to hear that song, and I believe in all of you that you’re going to help sing it.”

She sat back down as employees erupted in applause and the speakers filled with the guitar chords of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”

item.title: Jeff Bezos Says He Helped Pick Robert Pattinson as the New James Bond
item.description:
The Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said on Tuesday that he helped select Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond just days before the casting announcement this week.

Amazon acquired Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, the longtime home to the Bond franchise, in 2022 and has since gained creative control over future installments of the spy thriller series. The next film, starring Pattinson and directed by Denis Villeneuve, has no official release date but is expected to arrive in 2028 — closing what is on track to being the longest gap in the franchise’s history.

Bezos said he was “heavily involved” in the casting process, which had been shrouded in mystery. He was speaking at the Silicon Valley & The World conference hosted by the news outlet Semafor in Menlo Park, Calif.

He said the selection process began with a large group of candidates that was eventually whittled down to five finalists who recently performed screen tests in London. After final deliberations on Friday, Pattinson emerged as the top choice over Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner.

All five finalists were “extraordinarily talented,” Bezos said, “but there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.”

Initially, Bezos said, the selection group was hesitant about choosing Pattinson because he already had such a high profile.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” Bezos said. The Bond franchise has typically cast actors who were not yet A-listers.

“But in the screening tests, it was so obvious,” Bezos said. “He is James Bond.”

Pattinson, the “Twilight” breakout who has had a blockbuster year with roles in Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and Lance Oppenheim’s “Primetime,” will succeed Daniel Craig as the seventh actor to play 007 in the beloved series. Craig led five Bond films over 15 years, capping off his run in 2021 with “No Time to Die.”

“To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement,” Pattinson, 40, said in a statement to The New York Times.

Pattinson’s banner year is not over yet. Next month, he will appear in the star-studded final installment of Villeneuve’s “Dune” trilogy, joined by returning cast members Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya, Florence Pugh, Anya Taylor-Joy and Jason Momoa.

item.title: Fed Saw Need to Continue Raising Rates Despite October Skip
item.description:
Officials at the Federal Reserve broadly acknowledged the need to continue raising interest rates even as they voted against an increase at their October meeting, according to minutes from that gathering.

That record, released on Wednesday, indicated that for a few policymakers, October’s decisions was a “close call.” That reflected the heightened concern that many harbor about inflation, which has overshot the Fed’s 2 percent target for nearly six years. In recent months, price pressures have intensified more than expected even as the impact of President Trump’s tariffs have faded.

There was widespread recognition that the war with Iran and a surge in spending from artificial intelligence companies had made a broader range of goods and services more expensive.

“Several participants observed that tariff-related effects on prices appeared to be waning; however, most remarked that inflation pressures in the economy were broad based,” the minutes said. “The vast majority noted that high energy prices continued to contribute to current inflation pressures. Many participants observed that demand for products associated with the A.I. buildout was continuing to strain supply and raise prices of technology-related consumer goods, and several judged that price pressures were increasingly extending beyond industries directly affected by data center construction.”

The Fed’s decision to hold rates steady last month stemmed from a view adopted by several top policymakers that there was no urgency to rapidly lift borrowing costs after September’s quarter-point increase. That approach has been challenged in recent weeks as fresh consumer price data has affirmed that new sources of inflation appear to be cropping up across the economy.

Several officials have since embraced the need for swifter rate increases going forward, setting off an internal debate about just how fast to go. On Wednesday, Christopher J. Waller, a Fed governor, reiterated his view that the central bank should consider a half-point move when it next meets in December. In an interview with CNBC, he said it might be necessary to “shock people,” especially if the Fed did not explicitly signal that another rate increase in January was necessary.

John C. Williams, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, on Tuesday suggested that there was no need for “dramatic action,” even as he conceded that the central bank still had work to do on inflation. Instead, support seems to be coalescing around the idea of raising rates at consecutive meetings after a quarter-point increase next month. That would entail lifting borrowing costs again when the Fed meets at the end of January and then potentially doing so in mid-March if the data demanded it.

Some officials already supported a back-to-back cadence last month. Beth M. Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, and Lisa D. Cook, a central bank governor who is engaged in a protracted legal fight with President Trump over his efforts to oust her, dissented against a hold in favor of a quarter-point increase.

At a news conference after the rate decision, Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed chairman, stressed that the central bank had the flexibility to accrue more information about the state of the economy before taking additional steps to raise rates.

Mr. Warsh pointed to the fact that expectations about future inflation continued to show confidence in the Fed’s ability to return inflation to the 2 percent target. He also emphasized that credit conditions for households and businesses had become less favorable, which he said showed that “policy is working.”

U.S. stock markets have whipped around since the Fed last met. A.I. stocks have sold off sharply, first in the immediate wake of the midterm elections amid concerns that Democrats would usher in heightened regulatory scrutiny. More recently, they have buckled as a result of a shake-up at the chip maker Nvidia, whose chief executive, Jensen Huang, resigned after revelations that he had two affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence services determined was feeding information to Beijing.

U.S. borrowing costs have also climbed since the central bank’s October gathering. The 10-year Treasury note, which serves as a global benchmark, now trades around 5 percent, while the yield on two-year Treasuries, which are sensitive to changes in the Fed’s rate expectations, have surged to around 4.8 percent.

item.title: Social Media Helped Build Hailey Bieber’s Company. It Also Took a Mental Toll.
item.description:
Hailey Bieber, the model and entrepreneur who sold her Rhode beauty brand for at least $800 million last year, said that even though she had relied on social media to build her company and her online persona, it was “distorting” and had challenged her mental health.

“It can be distorting to the mind, especially those filters that change your face — they make your lips bigger, your nose smaller,” Mrs. Bieber said. “That definitely can be harmful and misleading, 100 percent. But it’s part of the world we’re living in; it’s not going anywhere.”

The 29-year-old is emblematic of two recent booms: the rise of the social-media-star-turned-entrepreneur and the popularity of skin care products, which has sent girls as young as 11 flocking to Sephora for serums.

Mrs. Bieber, who is married to the pop star Justin Bieber and is a daughter of the actor Stephen Baldwin, co-founded Rhode with Lauren and Michael D. Ratner in 2022 and sold it to E.L.F. Beauty for $800 million in cash and stock last year, with a potential payout of $200 million based on sales targets over three years.

Rhode — which is Mrs. Bieber’s middle name — has surged as E.L.F. introduced its products, like $20 peptide lip tints and a $32 glazing milk, at Sephora. Celebrity-backed brands run the risk of being flashes in the pan, a concern analysts brought up when the deal was announced, but Rhode has thrived so far.

That’s partly because of Mrs. Bieber, who has nearly 60 million Instagram followers and almost 20 million on TikTok. She remains the brand’s chief creative officer and head of innovation, and many of her online posts are devoted to marketing Rhode. (Mr. Bieber has also fueled her brand, referencing Rhode’s popular iPhone case with a slot that holds a lip gloss in a song.)

Mrs. Bieber said that social media had made her feel insecure and depressed in the past.

“I had people telling me to kill myself in the comments every single day,” she said. “The way people were making me feel was that maybe it would be better if I wasn’t here anymore, because that’s how intense I felt other people’s feelings were toward me.”

She said that she viewed the best path forward as “open conversation about what that looks like and how it might make somebody feel.”

item.title: Anthropic’s Public Debut Sets Up ‘Experiment’ in Corporate Power
item.description:
Todd Underwood, a former Anthropic engineering leader, fielded a stream of calls in recent months from investment managers eager to gain his insider view on the artificial intelligence giant’s business strategy ahead of this week’s initial public offering.

But few of the questions focused on an aspect of the company Mr. Underwood viewed as a crucial asset: Anthropic’s unusual governance structure.

The company is set to become by far the most valuable company on the stock market with the legal designation of a public benefit corporation, or P.B.C. That status requires Anthropic to prioritize its corporate mission — to develop safe A.I. systems “for the long-term benefit of humanity” — in addition to the customary sole focus on value for stockholders.

The company’s public benefit mandate is guarded partly by a five-member “long-term benefit trust,” which includes Ben Bernanke, the former Federal Reserve chair.

The company “will choose to do things in favor of safety rather than in favor of making money,” said Mr. Underwood, who has been sought out by investors as a former employee for insights into the company. He added that he agreed with that focus but thought it might turn off some investors.

The company’s public offering sets up an important test as Anthropic goes from one of the most closely watched private companies in the world to one of the most scrutinized.

Anthropic is expected to spend its first two years as a publicly traded company asking investors for patience as it burns hundreds of billions of dollars of cash to invest in new chips and data centers. It is also facing increasing calls from A.I. safety advocates, as well as some of its own employees, to slow down its pace of training new models.

On Wednesday, the company is expected to sell roughly $65 billion in shares, making it the second-largest I.P.O. after SpaceX’s earlier this year. It also has $26 billion of investments lined up from tech giants like Nvidia and Microsoft.

Anthropic’s expected market capitalization, more than $1.4 trillion, would make it 30 times as valuable as the next public benefit corporation that trades on the stock market, the software maker Veeva Systems.

Anthropic was founded as a public benefit corporation in 2021, and formed its long-term benefit trust in 2023 as a way to give the structure teeth, ensuring the company balances goals for shareholders and its broader mission. The structure is taxed the same as any corporation.

The trust is made up of a group of “financially disinterested” experts in economics, science and global health who don’t own Anthropic stock, the company said in its offering prospectus. The group has the power to appoint and remove several of the company’s board members, authority that is typically given only to shareholders.

Adding to the unusual leadership structure, the company also spent the months leading up to its public offering locking in new authority for the executives who started the company nearly six years ago, according to securities filings.

The company created a new class of shares this fall for its unusually large co-founding team — seven executives, including the chief executive, Dario Amodei — that give them 50.1 percent of voting control over the company, collectively. The founders have the ability to appoint other board members.

A founder-controlled board committee can also help overrule one of the trust’s four board appointments, reducing the trust’s power, said Jesse M. Fried, a Harvard law professor who has studied Anthropic’s corporate structure.

The trust’s authority was “watered down” as a result of the changes, but they don’t “fundamentally change the governance of the company,” he added.

Anthropic’s structure is unique when compared with other publicly traded companies, corporate governance experts said.

“I don’t know if I can really compare it to anything else,” said Douglas Chia, a senior fellow at Rutgers Law School who advises companies on corporate governance. “It’s going to be an interesting experiment.”

The Council of Institutional Investors, an advocacy group that represents public, union and corporate pension funds, has long been critical of arrangements that give founders voting control disproportionate to their financial stakes. The group wrote a letter this year expressing concerns that when SpaceX went public, it gave its founder, Elon Musk, dominant voting control.

The group will “wait and see” how Anthropic’s structure plays out, said Glenn Davis, the council’s executive director. The founders’ immense voting power means that “ultimately the founders are accountable to themselves,” rather than shareholders, he added.

The layered structure could still challenge investors’ understanding of the company and the group of people who govern it, said Paul Abrahimzadeh, a senior partner at the tech investment firm 1979 Capital.

Still, investor enthusiasm was inevitable despite the uncertainties, he added. “You have to own it. The question is at what price?”
